content.text: Salt traders measure distance in wells, not miles, which tells you plainly what the desert considers important. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.

A rumour from the last oasis reached us garbled, as rumours do, but garbled in a direction that turned out to be true. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household.

The caravan camped a half day short of the crossing rather than risk the flats in failing light. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family.

I have crossed the salt road twice now, and both times arrived a slightly different person than the one who set out. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory.

A guide's reputation rests entirely on wells that are there when he says they will be, and nothing else. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does.

The flats at midday are silent in a way that presses on the ears, absence made almost audible. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late.

We traded cloth for water at the last oasis, a rate the merchant called fair and I called fortunate. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed.

The salt road does not forgive confidence, only preparation, and even then only some of the time. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be.

The salt flats took the light and threw it back doubled, until the horizon stopped meaning anything in particular. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made.

A caravan at dusk moves slower than it does at noon, as though the animals too feel the day loosening its grip. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were.

The well at the crossing was half remembered by every guide who claimed to know it, which worried me more than an honest no. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument.

Merchants kept their ledgers in a shorthand no customs officer ever fully cracked, and none of them explained why. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was.

Rumour travelled faster across the flats than any caravan, arriving at the last oasis a full day ahead of us. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's.

The salt crust cracked under the camels' feet in a sound like distant, patient applause. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect.

A trader I met twice, years apart, told the same story both times with a different ending, and I preferred the second. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else. A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing.

At the last oasis the water tasted faintly of salt regardless, a joke the desert never tired of telling. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one.

The caravan master read the sky the way other men read a ledger, and trusted it about as much. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it.

A well half remembered is worse than a well forgotten outright, because it invites you to gamble on it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar.

We crossed the flats at night to spare the animals, and the stars there were more numerous than I had words for. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn.

The merchant's ledger recorded debts in three languages and grudges, I suspect, in a fourth known only to him. The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind.

The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning. A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed.

An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match.

The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting.

A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful.

The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change.

An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can.
